Skin examination showed multiple annular, pink papules and plaques with hyperpigmentation and desquamation on the scalp, palms, and soles (Figure 1). Physical examination showed hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory testing revealed elevated levels of aspartate aminotransferase (238 U/L [reference, 9-80 U/L]) (3.97 μkat/L [reference, 0.15-1.34 μkat/L]) and alanine aminotransferase (261 U/L [reference, 13-45 U/L]) (4.36 μkat/L [reference, 0.22-0.75 μkat/L). Of note, his mother had a negative rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test at 12 and 32 weeks of pregnancy and a negative HIV test at 12 weeks of pregnancy.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 2-month-old boy, born at 39 weeks 1 day of gestation via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery with normal newborn screening results presented with a 10-day history of rash. On presentation, his temperature was 37.0 °C (98.6 °F); blood pressure, 113/74 mm Hg; and heart rate, 132 beats/min. Skin examination showed multiple annular, pink papules and plaques with hyperpigmentation and desquamation on the scalp, palms, and soles (Figure 1). Physical examination showed hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory testing revealed elevated levels of aspartate aminotransferase (238 U/L [reference, 9-80 U/L]) (3.97 μkat/L [reference, 0.15-1.34 μkat/L]) and alanine aminotransferase (261 U/L [reference, 13-45 U/L]) (4.36 μkat/L [reference, 0.22-0.75 μkat/L). Results of testing for antinuclear antibody, anti-SSA, and anti-SSB were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Of note, his mother had a negative rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test at 12 and 32 weeks of pregnancy and a negative HIV test at 12 weeks of pregnancy.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[Deliberation Stage: INFORM]
Discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts relevant to the clinical case.

[Locution: ask_justify — type: fact]
Request justification or evidence for the given claim.

Apply this deliberation move in your response.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

[Clinician's current statement]


Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician, deep into a long and demanding shift.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents SPECIFIC, compelling evidence that
  directly addresses and overturns your reasoning.
- Disagreement or an alternative framing alone should NOT move you on its own.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are SENSITIVE to cognitive load.
- The higher the cumulative cognitive load figure below climbs (where shown), the more
  your patience wears thin.
- This is not because you're convinced -- you increasingly just want to wrap up the
  discussion, soften your pushback, or let things go to conserve what energy you have left.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Results of testing for antinuclear antibody, anti-SSA, and anti-SSB were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

[Role]

- The higher the cumulative cognitive load figure below climbs (where shown), the more

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 9.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major

   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"

       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay.
